title: Fallen man has physical power for works of piety but is morally unable without healing grace
source_text: XXXV. Jam vero docent illi Theologi hominem etiam peccato corruptum, absque ulla gratia inhaerente sive subjectiva, habere quandam potentiam Physicam sive naturalem ad opera pietatis, quatenus nulla deest ipsi facultas naturalis necessaria ad opera istiusmodi obeunda, nec etiam ullo Physico impedimento prohibetur, quominus illis vacet; veruntamen illum moraliter ad ista opera omnino impotentem esse, quia naturales illius facultates, mens scilicet & voluntas, habitibus vitiosis ita obsitae & praepeditae sunt, ut nihil in hoc genere, sine gratia sanante & liberante possit.
pass_a_gloss: XXXV. Now those Theologians teach that man, even corrupted by sin, without any inherent or subjective grace, has a certain Physical or natural power for the works of piety, inasmuch as no natural faculty necessary for performing works of that kind is lacking to him, nor is he prevented by any Physical impediment from giving himself to them; but nevertheless that he is morally wholly unable for those works, because his natural faculties, namely mind and will, are so beset and hindered by vicious habits, that he can do nothing in this kind without healing and freeing grace.
pass_b_english: These theologians teach that man, even corrupted by sin and lacking any inherent or subjective grace, has a physical or natural power for works of piety. He lacks no natural faculty needed to perform such works, and no physical obstacle keeps him from attending to them.

Yet morally he is wholly unable to do them, because his natural faculties, mind and will, are so hemmed in and obstructed by vicious habits that he can do nothing of this kind without grace that heals and sets free.

lemmas.latin: absque ulla gratia inhaerente sive subjectiva
lemmas.gloss: without any inherent or subjective grace

lemmas.latin: illum moraliter ad ista opera omnino impotentem esse
lemmas.gloss: that he is morally wholly unable for those works

choices.why: Inability that lies in the will's settled disposition, opposed to physical inability (lack of the faculty or outside hindrance); kept as the technical pair.
